ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) is a proliferative breast lesion with some, but not all, features of ductal carcinoma in situ. It confers a 4‑5‑fold increased risk of future breast cancer and may be a precursor to DCIS and invasive carcinoma.

sections.p: ADH is a focal proliferation of atypical epithelial cells within breast ducts that partially fills the ductal lumen and shows low‑grade cytologic atypia, but does not meet all criteria for DCIS.
b: Diagnosis requires core needle or excisional biopsy.
Criteria: ≤2 mm of contiguous involvement or ≤2 mm of total lesion size, and ≤1 mm of ductal space filled.

sections.p: ADH is not staged like invasive cancer; it is classified as a high‑risk lesion on the breast pathology spectrum.
b: Risk stratification: low‑risk (no ADH), moderate‑risk (ADH), high‑risk (DCIS, invasive cancer).

sections.p: ADH arises from genetic and hormonal influences that drive abnormal ductal proliferation.
b: BRCA2 mutation increases susceptibility.
Hormone exposure (early menarche, late menopause, hormone replacement).
Family history of breast cancer.

sections.p: Most patients are asymptomatic; ADH is usually discovered incidentally on imaging performed for another reason.
b: Mammographic microcalcifications (fine, linear, branching).
Occasional palpable mass if lesion is large.

sections.p: Imaging and tissue sampling confirm ADH and rule out more advanced disease.

t.b: Does the lesion show suspicious calcifications? → Presence suggests ADH/DCIS; absence may lower suspicion.
Is there a solid mass correlating with calcifications? → Helps guide biopsy; a cystic appearance argues against ADH.
What is the histology? → Shows partial ductal involvement with low‑grade atypia; confirms ADH.
Is there a pathogenic mutation? → Positive result raises long‑term risk and influences management.

sections.p: ADH itself is not malignant but signals a higher chance of progression to DCIS or invasive carcinoma.
b: Progression to DCIS if atypia expands beyond criteria.
Development of invasive ductal carcinoma, especially with BRCA2 mutation.

sections.p: Treatment balances removal of the lesion, risk reduction, and patient preferences.
b: Surgical excision of the core‑biopsy site to ensure complete removal.
Consider chemoprevention (selective estrogen receptor modulators or aromatase inhibitors) for risk reduction.
Avoid hormone replacement therapy in high‑risk women.

sections.p: Long‑term surveillance is essential because risk persists after excision.
b: Annual mammography; consider MRI if strong family history or BRCA mutation.
Lifestyle: maintain healthy weight, limit alcohol, regular exercise.

sections.p: ADH shares features with several other breast lesions.
b: Low‑grade DCIS – differs by extent of ductal involvement.
Flat epithelial atypia – lacks significant cytologic atypia.
Benign papilloma – shows papillary architecture, not atypical cells.

sections.p: Certain findings may give a false sense of security.
b: Small calcifications on mammography can be missed, leading to under‑diagnosis.
Core biopsy may underestimate lesion size; surgical excision may reveal more extensive disease.

whenToSeekHelp: New breast lump, skin changes, or nipple discharge accompanying imaging findings.

faq.a: No, ADH is a benign lesion but it raises the future risk of breast cancer.

faq.q: Do I need surgery for ADH?
faq.a: Complete excision of the area is recommended to rule out missed DCIS.
Selective estrogen receptor modulators or aromatase inhibitors can reduce the long‑term cancer risk.

exam: Describe the histologic criteria that differentiate ADH from low‑grade DCIS.
Explain why ADH confers a 4‑5‑fold increased risk of breast cancer and how this influences management.
List the recommended surveillance strategy after excision of ADH.
